title: Functions Calling Functions
objective: Compose functions by calling one from inside another, and trace how each call gets its own local scope.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Original Code Forge lesson connecting scope to function composition. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A function's body can call any other function that's already been defined, including ones you wrote yourself. This lets you break a problem into small, named pieces instead of writing one long block of code.

Each call — no matter which function it's in — gets its own fresh set of local variables. If sharpen_bonus() calls compute_rate(), compute_rate() cannot see sharpen_bonus()'s locals, and sharpen_bonus() cannot see compute_rate()'s locals either. The only thing that crosses the boundary is whatever compute_rate() returns.

This pattern — one function using another's return value — is how larger programs stay organized. Instead of one function doing everything, each function does one job and hands its result to whoever called it.
explanation.rule: Calling one function from inside another does not share their local variables — only a return value crosses that boundary.

examples.title: One Function Using Another's Result
examples.note: sharpen_bonus() calls compute_rate() and uses its return value, but never sees compute_rate()'s local variable 'base' as its own.

checks.question: function_a() calls function_b(). Can function_a() read a local variable created inside function_b()?
options: No — only function_b()'s return value crosses back to function_a().
Only if the variable has the same name in both functions.
Yes, but only after function_b() finishes.

feedback.correct: Correct — locals stay inside the function that created them; only the return value comes back.
feedback.incorrect: Locals never leak between functions, even when one calls the other. Only a return value crosses that boundary.

assignment.title: Bonus Calculator
assignment.brief: Write compute_rate(base) that returns base * 1.5, and sharpen_bonus(base) that calls compute_rate(base) and returns that result plus 10. Print sharpen_bonus(20).
requirements: Define sharpen_bonus(base) that calls compute_rate(base) and returns the result plus 10.
assignment.starterCode:

def sharpen_bonus(base):
    # Call compute_rate(base) and return the result plus 10.
    pass

print(sharpen_bonus(20))
